source.text:
tantrasāra, prathamam āhnikam
vimalakalāśrayābhinavasṛṣṭimahā jananī bharitatanuś ca pañcamukhaguptarucir janakaḥ /
tadubhayayāmalasphuritabhāvavisargamayaṃ hṛdayam anuttarāmṛtakulaṃ mama saṃsphuratāt // abhts_1.1 vitatas tantrāloko vigāhituṃ naiva śakyate sarvaiḥ /
ṛjuvacanaviracitam idaṃ tu tantrasāraṃ tataḥ śṛṇuta // abhts_1.2 śrīśambhunāthabhāskaracaraṇanipātaprabhāpagatasaṃkocam /
abhinavaguptahṛdambujam etad vicinuta maheśapūjanahetoḥ // abhts_1.3 iha jñānaṃ mokṣakāraṇaṃ bandhanimittasya ajñānasya virodhakatvāt dvividhaṃ ca ajñānaṃ buddhigataṃ pauruṣaṃ ca tatra buddhigatam aniścayasvabhāvaṃ viparītaniścayātmakaṃ ca / pauruṣaṃ tu vikalpasvabhāvaṃ saṃkucitaprathātmakaṃ tad eva ca mūlakāraṇaṃ saṃsārasya iti vakṣyāmo malanirṇaye / tatra pauruṣam ajñānaṃ dīkṣādinā nivartetāpi kiṃ tu dīkṣāpi buddhigate anadhyavasāyātmake ajñāne sati na sambhavati heyopādeyaniścayapūrvakatvāt tattvaśuddhiśivayojanārūpāyā dīkṣāyā iti / tatra adhyavasāyātmakaṃ buddhiniṣṭham eva jñānaṃ pradhānam tad eva ca abhyasyamānaṃ pauruṣam api ajñānaṃ nihanti vikalpasaṃvidabhyāsasya avikalpāntatāparyavasānāt / vikalpāsaṃkucitasaṃvitprakāśarūpo hy ātmā śivasvabhāva iti sarvathā samastavastuniṣṭhaṃ samyaṅniścayātmakaṃ jñānam upādeyam / tac ca śāstrapūrvakam / śāstraṃ ca parameśvarabhāṣitam eva pramāṇam / aparaśāstroktānām arthānāṃ tatra vaiviktyena abhyupagamāt tadarthātiriktayuktisiddhanirūpaṇāc ca tena aparāgamoktaṃ jñānaṃ tāvata eva bandhāt vimocakam na sarvasmāt sarvasmāt tu vimocakaṃ parameśvaraśāstraṃ pañcasrotomayaṃ daśāṣṭādaśavasvaṣṭabhedabhinnam / tato 'pi sarvasmāt sāraṃ ṣaḍardhaśāstrāṇi / tebhyo 'pi mālinīvijayam / tadantargataś cārthaḥ saṃkalayyāśakyo nirūpayitum /
na ca anirūpitavastutattvasya muktatvaṃ mocakatvaṃ vā śuddhasya jñānasyaiva tathārūpatvāt iti /
svabhyastajñānamūlatvāt parapuruṣārthasya tatsiddhaye idam ārabhyate /
ajñānaṃ kila bandhahetur uditaḥ śāstre malaṃ tat smṛtaṃ pūrṇajñānakalodaye tad akhilaṃ nirmūlatāṃ gacchati /
dhvastāśeṣamalātmasaṃvidudaye mokṣaś ca tenāmunā śāstreṇa prakaṭīkaromi nikhilaṃ yaj jñeyatattvaṃ bhavet // abhts_1.4 tatra iha svabhāva eva paramopādeyaḥ sa ca sarvabhāvānāṃ prakāśarūpa eva aprakāśasya svabhāvatānupapatteḥ sa ca nānekaḥ prakāśasya taditarasvabhāvānupraveśāyoge svabhāvabhedābhāvāt deśakālāv api ca asya na bhedakau tayor api tatprakāśasvabhāvatvāt iti eka eva prakāśaḥ sa eva ca saṃvit arthaprakāśarūpā hi saṃvit iti sarveṣām atra avivāda eva / sa ca prakāśo na paratantraḥ prakāśyataiva hi pāratantryam prakāśyatā ca prakāśāntarāpekṣitaiva na ca prakāśāntaraṃ kiṃcit asti iti svatantra ekaḥ prakāśaḥ svātantryād eva ca deśakālākārāvacchedavirahāt vyāpako nityaḥ sarvākāranirākārasvabhāvaḥ tasya ca svātantryam ānandaśaktiḥ taccamatkāra icchāśaktiḥ prakāśarūpatā cicchaktiḥ āmarśātmakatā jñānaśaktiḥ sarvākārayogitvaṃ kriyāśaktiḥ ity evaṃ mukhyābhiḥ śaktibhiḥ yukto 'pi vastuta icchājñānakriyāśaktiyuktaḥ anavacchinnaḥ prakāśo nijānandaviśrāntaḥ śivarūpaḥ sa eva svātantryāt ātmānaṃ saṃkucitam avabhāsayan aṇur iti ucyate /
punar api ca svātmānaṃ svatantratayā prakāśayati yena anavacchinnaprakāśaśivarūpatayaiva prakāśate /
tatrāpi svātantryavaśāt anupāyam eva svātmānaṃ prakāśayati sopāyaṃ vā sopāyatve 'pi icchā vā jñānaṃ vā kriyā vā abhyupāya iti traividhyaṃ śāmbhavaśāktāṇavabhedena samāveśasya tatra caturvidham api etad rūpaṃ krameṇa atra upadiśyate /
ātmā prakāśavapur eṣa śivaḥ svatantraḥ svātantryanarmarabhasena nijaṃ svarūpam /
saṃchādya yat punar api prathayeta pūrṇaṃ tac ca kramākramavaśād athavā tribhedāt // abhts_1.5

l1_text:
## tsa01-p01
Stainless-art-abode, great new creation — the Mother; full-bodied, the Father of hidden splendor with five faces: may the Heart, which is the emission-nature of the throbbing being sprung from the couple of those two, the unsurpassed deathless clan, flash forth for me. (1.1) The Tantrāloka is vast — not everyone can plunge into it; so listen to this Tantrasāra, composed in plain words. (1.2) This lotus-heart of Abhinavagupta, its contraction gone through the splendor of the falling feet of Śambhunātha Bhāskara — pick it, for the worship of Maheśa. (1.3) Here, knowledge is the cause of liberation, through being the opponent of ignorance, the cause of bondage. And ignorance is twofold: intellect-located and personal. Therein, the intellect-located is doubt-natured and wrong-conviction-natured; the personal is thought-natured and contracted-manifestation-natured — and that itself is the root cause of saṃsāra, as we shall teach under the determination of stain. Therein, personal ignorance may be removed by initiation and the rest; but initiation itself is not possible while intellect-located non-determination-natured ignorance persists — since initiation, of the form of purification of principles and joining to Śiva, is preceded by determination of what to shun and take. Hence determinative, intellect-abiding knowledge alone is principal; and that itself, being practiced, kills personal ignorance too — since practice of thought-consciousness ends in the thought-free. For the self, thought-contracted-consciousness-light-natured, is Śiva-natured. Hence in all cases, all-thing-directed, right-determination-natured knowledge is to be adopted. And that is scripture-preceded; and scripture is authority only as Lord-spoken — since the things taught by others' scriptures are accepted therein discriminatively, and since there is reason-proved exposition beyond their content. Hence knowledge taught by another āgama liberates from bondage only so far, not from all; but the Lord's scripture liberates from all — five-streamed, differentiated into ten, eighteen, eight, and the rest. Than all that, the essence is the sixfold scriptures; than those, the Mālinīvijaya; and its contained content, gathered, is impossible to expound. Nor is there freedom or liberating power for one whose thing-nature is unexpounded — since only pure knowledge is so natured. Since the supreme goal is rooted in well-practiced knowledge, for its success this is begun. Ignorance, declared in scripture the cause of bondage — that is called stain; at the rise of the digit of full knowledge, all that goes to rootlessness. When self-consciousness rises with destroyed remainderless stains, there is liberation too; hence by this man, with scripture, I reveal entirely whatever knowable reality there may be. (1.4) Therein, here, own nature alone is supremely adoptable; and it is light-nature of all things — since non-light cannot be nature. And it is not many — since there is no entry of other natures into light, since there is no difference of nature. And place and time too are not dividers of it — since they too are light-natured. Hence there is one light alone; and it alone is consciousness — since consciousness is of the nature of thing-manifestation — and here, for all, there is no dispute. And that light is not dependent — since being-illumined is dependence, and since illuminedness needs another light, and since no other light at all exists. Hence there is the autonomous one light — through autonomy alone, free from limitation by place, time, and form, all-pervading, eternal, all-form-formless-natured. Of it, autonomy is bliss-power; its wonder is will-power; light-nature is consciousness-power; grasp-nature is knowledge-power; all-form-fitness is action-power. Thus, though endowed with chief powers, really will-knowledge-action-powered, unlimited light resting in own bliss is Śiva-natured. He alone, through autonomy, manifesting himself contracted, is called atom. And again he manifests his own self autonomously — whereby he shines as unlimited-light-Śiva-nature itself. There too, through autonomy, he manifests his own self without means or with means; and even with means — will, knowledge, or action as approach — hence threefoldness of immersion, by śāmbhava, śākta, āṇava distinction. Therein, all four forms too are here taught in order. The self, light-bodied, this Śiva, autonomous — by the force of autonomy's play, having hidden his own nature, whatever he would spread forth again, full — that, by force of sequence-and-nosequence, or by threefoldness. (1.5)
l2_text:
## tsa01-p01 — one's own nature
Abhinavagupta opens in praise: the Mother of stainless art and new creation, the full-bodied Father of five hidden faces — may the Heart they throb forth, the deathless clan beyond all, flash for me. The Tantrāloka is an ocean few can dive; so hear its essence, said plainly. And reader — gather this lotus-heart of Abhinavagupta, opened by his master's feet, for the worship of the Great Lord.
The teaching begins with a clean cut. Knowledge frees because it opposes exactly what binds: not-knowing. And not-knowing is two things. One sits in the intellect — doubt, and being sure of the wrong thing. The other sits in the person — the churn of thoughts, awareness pulled tight. That second one is saṃsāra's root (its full account comes with the stains). Initiation can wash the personal kind — but initiation itself needs you to already tell shun from take, to be purified and joined to Śiva; while the intellect still can't decide, no initiation is possible. So first comes first: clear, deciding, intellect-dwelling knowledge. Practice that, and it finishes the other job too, since practised thought ends where thought ends. For what you are — awareness squeezed into thoughts, but light by nature — is Śiva already. So in every case, adopt knowledge that decides rightly about everything. And that knowledge comes led by scripture — scripture that counts being Lord-spoken, since it takes whatever lesser books say, keeps it discriminately, and out-argues the rest. Lesser revelations free you partway; only the Lord's word — five streams, ten, eighteen, eight and all their branches — frees altogether. Its essence: the sixfold books; theirs: the Mālinīvijaya, whose content no gathering can exhaust. Nobody is free, or frees, without the nature of things spelled out — only pure knowing does that. And since man's highest end stands on practised knowing, this book begins here to secure it. Scripture calls ignorance bondage's cause, stain by name; when full knowledge dawns entire, it goes rootless; when self-awareness rises with every stain destroyed, there is freedom too — so with this book I lay open all there is to know.
And here is the one thing to take hold of: your own nature. It can only be light — what doesn't shine can't be what a thing is. It can only be one — nothing alien gets into light, so natures can't differ; and place and time don't cut it either, being light themselves. So: one light, which is awareness — awareness just is things showing up, and no one disputes it. And it depends on nothing — to be lit is to depend, and depending needs another light, and there is none. So the one light is free: unbounded by place, time, or shape, everywhere, always, every shape and none. Its freedom is bliss; its wonder, will; its shining, consciousness; its grasp, knowledge; its fitting every shape, action. Chief powers in display, three in truth — will, knowing, doing — the boundless light resting in its own bliss is Śiva. Contracting himself by that same freedom, he is called the atom. Then, freely still, he shows himself again as boundless Śiva-light. And that showing goes with means or without: will, knowing, or doing as the way in — three immersions, śāmbhava, śākta, of the atom — and a fourth besides; all four taught here in turn. The self is Śiva, light-bodied, free — hiding his own nature in freedom's play, then spreading it whole again, whether step by step, all at once, or three ways at once.
*Fidelity: preserved (maṅgala trio, two ignorances + initiation logic, śāstra hierarchy, one-light proof, five→three powers, contraction, four means). Added: "arithmetic" none; SUPPLIED-minor: "for the worship of the Great Lord" purpose-phrase kept literal (maheśapūjanahetoḥ). Not-resolved: Mālinīvijaya inexhaustibility (external).*

c1.body:
Abhinavagupta opens with a maṅgala invoking his parents — Mother of stainless art and new creation, Father of hidden splendor with five faces — promising the Tantrasāra as the plain-words distillation of the vast Tantrāloka, then enters the teaching: knowledge, not ritual, is liberation's cause, because it opposes ignorance, the cause of bondage. Ignorance is twofold — intellectual (doubt and wrong conviction) and personal (thought-natured, contracted; saṃsāra's root). Initiation can wash the personal kind, but initiation itself requires prior intellectual determination, so determinative knowledge comes first. Scripture alone fully authorizes, absorbing lesser revelations discriminatively. Own nature is one autonomous light — the same in all things, unbounded by place, time, or form — whose contraction is bondage (the atom) and whose expansion is freedom; autonomy itself is bliss, will, consciousness, knowledge, action. Re-manifestation runs sudden or gradual, with or without means — will, knowledge, action as the three approaches (śāmbhava/śākta/āṇava), and a fourth.

The passage moves in four steps, each building on the last. First, the epistemic diagnosis: bondage is not a thing but a not-knowing, and not-knowing has two seats — the intellect that cannot decide (doubt, wrong conviction) and the person whose awareness is pulled tight into thoughts. Initiation, which removes the personal kind, presupposes the intellectual kind's removal, so determinative knowledge is principal; practised, it finishes the other job too, since thought-practice ends in thought-free awareness. For what you are — awareness squeezed into thoughts, but light by nature — is Śiva already. So in every case, adopt knowledge that decides rightly about everything. Second, the authority claim: scripture that counts is Lord-spoken, since it takes whatever lesser books say, keeps it discriminatively, and out-argues the rest. Lesser revelations free you partway; only the Lord's word — five streams, ten, eighteen, eight and all their branches — frees altogether. Its essence runs pañcasrotas → ṣaḍardha → Mālinīvijaya, whose content no gathering can exhaust. Nobody is free, or frees, without the nature of things spelled out — only pure knowing does that. And since man's highest end stands on practised knowing, this book begins here to secure it. Third, the ontological core: own nature can only be light (what doesn't shine can't be what a thing is), and only one light (nothing alien enters light, so natures can't differ; place and time are themselves light), and autonomous (illuminedness needs another light; none exists) — hence all-pervading, eternal, every form and none. Autonomy is bliss; wonder, will; shining, consciousness; grasp, knowledge; fitting every form, action — really three powers (will, knowing, doing). Contracted, that light is the atom; free, it is Śiva. Fourth, the fourfold means previewed: sudden or gradual re-manifestation, with or without means — will, knowledge, action as the three approaches, plus a fourth.
c1.terms: jñāna (knowledge, liberation's cause), ajñāna (ignorance, twofold: buddhigata + pauruṣa), mala (stain, saṃsāra's root), svabhāva (own nature = prakāśa), svātantrya (autonomy = ānanda), prakāśa (light = saṃvit), aṇu (atom = contracted self), samāveśa (immersion, threefold: śāmbhava/śākta/āṇava).
c1.see_also: A02 (anupāya), A05 (āṇava), essay0 Q1 ("What is my own nature?"), spans TS1.4/TS9.2/TS21.1/TS22.1.
c1.function: Opens the whole work: establishes the problem (ignorance), the authority (Lord-spoken scripture), the one reality (autonomous light), and the fourfold means that the next four ahnikas will teach.
c1.local_context: First ahnika; follows the maṅgala (1.1–1.3); precedes A02 (anupāya, the means-less immersion).
c1.boundary: Mala specifics deferred (malanirṇaye). Upāya details deferred to A02–A05. Mālinīvijaya's inexhaustibility is Abhinava's claim, not argued here. The maṅgala's parent-imagery is invocatory, not doctrinal.
